title: Would you make this interaction event-driven or request-response?
summary: Tests whether you pick based on whether the caller needs an answer now versus just needs the side effect to eventually happen — and can name the coupling trade-off underneath either choice.

slides.markdown:
Underneath this question is a coupling trade-off: request-response keeps the caller in control of the outcome but ties it directly to the callee's availability and latency; event-driven frees the caller but gives up its ability to know what happened next.

A good answer picks based on whether the caller genuinely needs the result to proceed, not on which style feels more modern.

Ask: **does the initiating flow need the result to proceed, or just needs to know the action was accepted?** And: **how many other services need to react to this same event?**

A single downstream dependency that must respond before the caller continues points toward request-response; multiple independent reactors, none of which the caller blocks on, point toward events.

**Request-response** when the caller blocks on the result. **Event-driven** when it doesn't, and/or when multiple independent parties need to react to the same thing happening.

The test isn't "is this action synchronous by nature" — it's whether the *caller's own flow* needs the answer to move forward.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: checkout's two different needs
slides.markdown:
| Interaction | Caller blocks on result? | Right shape |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory check before showing "in stock" | Yes — UI can't proceed without the answer | Request-response |
| Notifying shipping, billing, analytics that an order was placed | No — none of them block checkout | Event-driven |

The same checkout flow contains both — the shape is a property of the interaction, not the whole system.

Adding fraud-scoring as a new consumer of the "order placed" flow shows the difference starkly. With events, it's a new subscriber to an existing topic — zero changes to checkout's code. With request-response, checkout's code has to grow a new synchronous call to the fraud service, adding its latency and its failure mode to every single checkout.

This is the concrete case for event-driven fan-out: adding a reactor shouldn't require touching the thing that triggered it.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the coupling cost that comes with event-driven
slides.markdown:
The flip side: checkout no longer knows or controls what happens downstream, which is the point — but it also means checkout can't answer "did the fraud check pass" synchronously if a later requirement needs that.

Decoupling isn't free even when it's exactly what you wanted; it removes a capability (synchronous visibility) along with the coupling.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: request-response chain vs pub/sub fan-out
slides.markdown:
![Synchronous call chain versus one event fanning out to independent subscribers](assets/chain-vs-fanout.svg)

The chain on the left has a single path that can break at any link; the fan-out on the right has none of the subscribers depending on each other at all.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Event-driven buys loose coupling and easy fan-out at the cost of end-to-end traceability — you can no longer follow one causal chain in a single trace without deliberately stitching it back together across services.

Request-response keeps that single trace for free, but every synchronous hop you add becomes a new point of failure and latency on the caller's critical path. Neither is strictly better; they trade different things.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you debug a silent failure across 5 event-driven services?
slides.markdown:
**Correlation IDs** propagated through every event, plus **distributed tracing** that spans the async boundary — most tracing tools (e.g., OpenTelemetry) support attaching trace context to a message so a consumer picks up the same trace the producer started.

Without this, five loosely-coupled services and a silent no-op is genuinely hard to root-cause; with it, you can still walk the causal chain even though there's no single synchronous call stack to follow.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a single order-status view spanning all five services
slides.markdown:
Build a **materialized view / read model** that subscribes to all five services' events and aggregates state into one place, rather than reverting to synchronous calls to each service on every status check.

This keeps the event-driven decoupling for the write path while giving the read path a single, fast place to answer "what's the status of order 4471" without querying five services live.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: picking one style for everything
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "our architecture is event-driven" or "our architecture is synchronous" as a blanket rule for every interaction.

**Why it's wrong:** making everything event-driven loses the ability to reason about a request's end-to-end outcome where you actually needed it; chaining everything synchronously couples services that should have been decoupled and adds unnecessary latency and failure surface.

**Correct model:** decide per interaction, based on whether the caller blocks on the result — the same system legitimately has both.

Request-response when the caller blocks on the result; event-driven when it doesn't, or when multiple independent parties need to react. Name the trade-off — traceability versus coupling — and know the fixes for its downsides: correlation IDs plus tracing for debugging, and a materialized view for cross-service status without going back to synchronous calls.

The deeper mechanics of building an event-driven system are covered in [event-driven architecture](event-driven-architecture).
